finding: §4's emission condition and §4's bucket invariant are mutually exclusive, so the invariant can never be observed on an emitted key and §7 test 17 has no constructible fixture. The condition: by_severity is emitted only when "the merged round would be clean under the resolved policy AND holds at least one non-PASS row". The invariant: "error + unrecognised sums the round's blocking rows". §2 makes unrecognised blocking ("An unrecognised severity is treated as blocking") and error blocking ("Blocking severity is error"). A round clean under blocking therefore has zero blocking rows by definition, so on every round where by_severity is emitted, error + unrecognised is identically 0 and the sum carries no information. Test 17 asks for the assertion "over a fixture carrying all four unrecognised shapes" -- four blocking rows -- which is exactly a round that is NOT clean under blocking, so by_severity is absent and the test cannot read the buckets it asserts over. An implementer must invent one of: emit on unclean rounds too, exempt unrecognised from blocking, or drop the sum. Falsifier checked: §4 would have to state a second emission case, or §2 would have to grade unrecognised as non-blocking. §4 line 183-184 states one condition only; §2 line 64-66 states the fail-closed rule normatively.
suggestion: Split the two claims and state both. Replace the closing clause of §4's bucket paragraph with: "error + unrecognised is the round's blocking-row count, which is 0 on every round that carries the key -- the invariant is what makes that zero readable rather than a coincidence of one implementation. It is asserted on the counter itself, not on an emitted payload." And rewrite §7 row 17 to: "| 17 | §4 *buckets* | the by_severity counter over a round carrying all four unrecognised shapes puts every one in `unrecognised`, so error + unrecognised equals that round's blocking-row count -- asserted on the counter directly, since such a round is not clean under blocking and so carries no emitted key | a \"\" bucket, or splitting the four |"

finding: §3's "resolved, not stored" paragraph mandates a refusal for a case that cannot occur under §2's stated precedence, and misses the one write that CAN produce it. §3 requires: "a --project write of `all` that *uncovers* a task override of `blocking` changes the resolved value and must be refused." Under §2's precedence (task override > project config > built-in) a task override of blocking already wins, so writing anything at the project layer leaves the resolved value at blocking -- no change, nothing to refuse -- and neither setter has an unset form (read internal/cli/set.go:325-506 and internal/cli/set_project.go:22-120: every branch assigns a value; there is no delete or empty-value path). So an implementer told to make this refuse cannot construct an input. The reachable instance is `tp import`: internal/cli/importcmd.go:158 carries the existing workflow block forward only when the imported document has NO top-level `workflow` key (importedHasWorkflowKey is a raw-JSON top-level key check); an imported document that DOES carry a workflow block omitting audit_converge_on replaces the block and drops a task-level `all`, uncovering a project-level `blocking`. That write names neither literal, so an implementer following §3's three enumerated shapes (a literal blocking, all-then-blocking, an import carrying blocking forward) ships the hole. §3's table row 1 also misstates import: it carries forward when the DOCUMENT omits the workflow key, not when it omits the field.
suggestion: Replace the impossible example and fix the table row. §3's paragraph should read: "'Resolved' means resolved, not stored at the written layer. A --project write of `blocking` under a task override of `all` changes nothing an audit will read, and must pass. The refusal is not always a write of `blocking`: an import whose workflow block is present but omits the field drops a task-level `all` and uncovers a project-level `blocking`, changing the resolved value without naming either literal, and is refused. The comparison is resolved-before against resolved-after, at every sink, over the whole block a sink writes rather than over the keys it names." §3's table row 1's `fails on` cell should say "...carries the existing block forward only when the imported DOCUMENT omits the top-level workflow key; a present-but-partial block drops the field." Add a §7 row: "| 13b | §3 *the change rule* | an import whose workflow block is present and omits the field, over a task-level `all` and a project-level `blocking`, is refused under TP_UNATTENDED=1 | a fence that compares only the keys the write names |"

finding: §4 asserts "`--merge` can evaluate that condition -- it holds the round's rows and resolves the same field `--record` will", and that is not buildable: `--merge` has no spec argument, and `--record`'s resolution is keyed on one. Measured in the tree: `runAuditMerge(args []string, outputPath string)` (internal/cli/audit_merge.go:19) takes only NDJSON paths and rejects a spec-looking positional at entry with exit 2 (lines 29-38); `runAuditRecord` resolves with `engine.ResolveWorkflow(specPath, flagFile)` (audit_record.go:44,91), and `ResolveWorkflow` (internal/engine/workflow_resolve.go:16-36) uses the spec THREE times -- it accepts the discovered task file only when `specMatches(tfPath, tf.Spec, specPath)`, then falls back to `SpecAdjacentTaskFile(specPath)`, then to project-only. So `--merge`, which can only reach `DiscoverTaskFile(".", flagFile)`, resolves a different layer stack from `--record` exactly when the active task file's `spec` field is not the spec being audited -- which is the normal state in this repository, where fourteen `spec/*.tasks.json` files sit beside one `.tp/local.json` active pointer. The result is a key that appears or disappears on `--merge` disagreeing with the `clean` `--record` stamps one command later, which is the opposite of the readability §1 deliverable 3 promises.
suggestion: State the input. Add to §4, after "`--merge` can evaluate that condition": "It resolves the field from the same two layers `--record` does, but without a spec it cannot use `ResolveWorkflow`'s spec-matching path. `--merge` therefore takes the spec it is merging for: `tp audit <spec> --merge <a.ndjson> ...` -- the positional §4.1 currently refuses -- OR the release states that `--merge` resolves through the discovered task file and its project config alone, and §7 gains a row pinning the case where the two disagree." Whichever is chosen, add a §7 row: "| 15b | §4 | `--merge` and the `--record` that follows it resolve the same value when the active task file's `spec` field names a different spec | resolving `--merge` through task-file discovery while `--record` resolves through the spec |"

finding: §7's premise is "Every test here is derived from a numbered decision above, and the derivation is written down", and row 4 has no such decision. Row 4 cites "§2 *The field*" and asserts "`tp config --extract` emits the field; `tp validate --project` accepts a legal value and rejects an illegal one". §2 *The field* (lines 42-45) says only: the value set, the resolution precedence, and refusal at the write and consuming sinks. Neither `tp config --extract` nor `tp validate --project` appears anywhere in §2, §2.1, §3, §4 or §6a -- the row's stated justification is a history note ("v0.31.0 shipped the twin without both and needed v0.31.1"), not a decision this spec makes. This is the failure the derivation column exists to expose, in the direction the column cannot catch: the column is checked by reading down from §7, and a row citing a real anchor that does not carry the claim reads as covered. It matters for building because the two commands are real work -- internal/cli/config_extract.go's `computeCommonPolicy`, `hoistedFields` and `mergeCommon` each need a new line, and internal/cli/validate_project.go needs a deviation branch -- and nothing normative in the spec asks for any of it.
suggestion: Give the row a decision to derive from. Add to §2 *The field*, after the sink sentence: "The field is a project-config field like its twin, so it is hoisted by `tp config --extract` and reported by `tp validate --project` when a task override deviates from the project value. v0.31.0 shipped `review_converge_on` without both and needed v0.31.1 to add them; this release ships them together." Then row 4's `derives from` cell reads "§2 *The field*" truthfully.

finding: §2 decides what `clean` means under `blocking` and leaves `findings` -- the field `clean` is computed from today and the field §7 test 10 needs -- undecided, so two observably different implementations both satisfy the spec. In the tree `clean := findings == 0` (internal/cli/audit_record.go:71) and `findings` is both an emitted top-level key (line 99) and a stored round field (`engine.ReviewRound.Findings`, recordAuditRoundEntry line 207). Under `blocking` the two must separate, and §2 never says which way: either `findings` keeps counting every non-PASS row and `clean` is computed beside it, or `findings` becomes policy-aware and reports 0 on an accepted-open round. §2's boundary paragraph names exactly three fields that stay severity-blind -- `role_streaks[].open`, its `consecutive_clean`, and `spec_coverage_clean_rounds` -- and §7's closing "Not tested here, named so the absence is deliberate" paragraph repeats the same three. `findings` is in neither list. It is not a cosmetic choice: §2 requires `next_action` to name "how many non-PASS rows were accepted" and §7 test 10 pins that number, and on the `--status` path (audit_record.go:390) the only source for it is the latest stored round's `Findings` -- which is zero under the second reading, leaving test 10 unimplementable there.
suggestion: Decide it in §2, in the boundary paragraph. Change "`role_streaks[].open`, its `consecutive_clean` and `spec_coverage_clean_rounds` stay severity-blind" to "`findings` -- both the emitted key and the value stored on the round -- keeps counting every non-`PASS` row under both values, so `clean` and `findings` separate under `blocking` and the accepted count `next_action` names is readable from a stored round without re-reading its rows. `role_streaks[].open`, its `consecutive_clean` and `spec_coverage_clean_rounds` stay severity-blind for the same reason." Then add the same field to §7's closing paragraph or give it a row: "| 10b | §2 *next_action* | a round recorded clean under `blocking` still stores and emits `findings` equal to its non-`PASS` row count, which is where `--status` reads the accepted count | making `findings` policy-aware, which zeroes the number test 10 asserts |"

finding: §7 row 7's fourth column is `—`, and §7's own opening makes that column the point of the table: "column 4 naming the input that makes it fail", with the stated cost of the old list being that it "went from 14 of 14 writable and 11 discriminating to 12 and 8". A row that declares no falsifying input declares itself non-discriminating, which by §7's own standard is a row that should not be in the list. The input exists and is easy to name -- an implementation that blocks only on the unrecognised bucket, or one that grades `error` by the review ranker (`engine.SeverityRank`, internal/engine/cluster.go:36, which ranks `error` as unknown(4) alongside `warning` and `info`) -- so the em dash is an unfinished cell rather than a true absence. It also loses the one decision in §2 that no other row derives from: "the audit predicate does not reuse the review ranker -- one that did would rank every audit severity as unknown".
suggestion: Fill the cell with the decision it is missing: "| 7 | §2 *Blocking severity is `error`* | `error` blocks under both values, and the predicate does not go through the review ranker | grading the audit row with `engine.SeverityRank`, which ranks `error`, `warning` and `info` alike as unknown |"

finding: §2.1 places a normative documentation obligation on the release -- "`skills/tp/SKILL.md` carries the one-line command that derives it, next to the field's documentation, so the decision has a stated basis rather than a suggestion to go and look" -- and no §7 row derives from it, while §7's closing paragraph ("Not tested here, named so the absence is deliberate") lists only `role_streaks[].open`, its `consecutive_clean` and `spec_coverage_clean_rounds`. So the clause is neither tested nor declared deliberately untested, which is exactly the hole the derivation column was added to expose. It is testable the way the release already tests documents: internal/cli/docs_contract_test.go asserts pinned substrings over `readRepoDoc(t, "skills/tp/SKILL.md")` today (lines 131-135), and §7 row 19 already reaches SKILL.md for §6a. It is also the clause most likely to be dropped, because it is the only deliverable in the release with no Go code behind it.
suggestion: Add a §7 row: "| 4b | §2.1 *the release owes the operator that number* | `skills/tp/SKILL.md` documents the field and, beside it, the one-line command that counts `severity` across a cycle's `audit-round-*.ndjson` -- asserted as a pinned substring through the docs-contract guard | documenting the field with no way to get the number the decision is made on |" -- or, if it is deliberately untested, name it in §7's closing "Not tested here" paragraph so the absence is a decision rather than an omission.

finding: §7 uses "the corpus" for two different populations two paragraphs apart, and the number an implementer would have to reproduce belongs to the one the fixture does not contain. Row 6 justifies asserting `warning` separately with "158 of the corpus's 360 non-PASS rows"; the paragraph under the table defines the replay fixture as "The 22 recorded round files ... 3,046 rows". I counted both over spec/.tp-review/ with a python3 walk: 158/360 is the whole 90-file audit corpus across every spec; the 22 files of v0.35.0 and v0.36.0 hold 3,046 rows (exactly as stated) of which 133 are non-PASS and 66 are `warning`. So a unit that builds the fixture §7 specifies and then checks row 6's stated reason against it finds 66/133 and cannot tell whether the fixture is wrong, the number is stale, or the two sentences mean different things. Every other measured number in the release reproduced exactly against the tree (v0.35.0's 42 non-PASS as 3/22/17; 2,913 PASS rows all with `severity: null`; 67 outside-enum rows in 15 files across v0.29.0-v0.32.0; the §2.1 table at both `audit_clean_rounds` values), which is what makes this one worth naming rather than the numbers in general.
suggestion: Name the population in row 6: "| 6 | §2 table | `warning` is advisory -- asserted separately from `info`, since it is 158 of the 360 non-`PASS` rows in tp's whole recorded audit corpus, and 66 of the 133 in this release's replay fixture | a predicate that special-cases `info` |" Adding the fixture's own figure makes the row checkable against the artifact the test actually commits.

finding: §3 closes an enumeration -- "The three write paths are `tp set --workflow`, its `--project` form, and `tp import`" -- and there is a fourth command that writes both workflow layers. I counted the writers with faster_search over internal/cli: `engine.WriteProjectConfig` has exactly two call sites, set_project.go:195 and config_extract.go:298, and `engine.StripTaskWorkflowFields` has one, config_extract.go:304. So `tp config --extract` writes the project block AND removes the field from every task file, and it already handles the twin (`computeCommonPolicy` line 71, `hoistedFields` line 131, `mergeCommon` line 182). It is resolution-preserving in the case it fires -- `commonPtr` hoists only a value every task file sets identically -- but that is a fact an implementer has to derive, and §3's fence is defined on resolved-before vs resolved-after "at every sink", so a reader has to decide whether `runConfigExtract` is a sink that needs the comparison wired in. Nothing in `runConfigExtract` reads TP_UNATTENDED today.
suggestion: Say four and say why the fourth needs nothing: "The write paths are `tp set --workflow`, its `--project` form, `tp import`, and `tp config --extract`. The first three are fenced. `--extract` hoists only a value every task file already sets identically and strips it from those files in the same write, so resolved-before equals resolved-after by construction and it carries no fence -- stated here so the absence is a decision rather than an oversight." Add a §7 row asserting it: "| 12b | §3 *the change rule* | `tp config --extract` hoisting a unanimous `blocking` leaves the resolved value unchanged and is not refused under `TP_UNATTENDED=1` | fencing every writer of the field rather than every write that changes what resolves |"

finding: Three of §7's nineteen `derives from` cells name a clause the spec does not carry under that name, which weakens the mechanism the section was rewritten around ("a decision that changes and leaves its row untouched is visible" only works if the pointer resolves). I checked each cell against the section text. Row 14 cites "§3 *escalation*": the word escalation does not appear anywhere in §3 -- the clause is the paragraph headed "**The refusal is nameable.**". Row 8 cites "§2 *unrecognised*", but the four shapes it asserts ("outside the enum, `null`, absent, or not a string") are enumerated in §4's bucket paragraph, not in §2, which says only "An unrecognised severity is treated as blocking" -- so the row derives from two clauses and names one, and an edit to §4's four shapes would leave row 8 visibly untouched. Row 9b cites "§2 *stamped*" while its content ("the relaxing direction") is the separate paragraph headed "**Stamping is symmetric and the relaxing direction is the one to state.**", which row 9 also points at.
suggestion: Repoint the three cells at the paragraph lead-ins the spec actually carries: row 14 to "§3 *The refusal is nameable*"; row 8 to "§2 *unrecognised* + §4 *buckets*", since the four shapes are §4's; row 9b to "§2 *Stamping is symmetric*". Then add one sentence under the table: "A cell names the bolded lead-in of the paragraph it derives from, verbatim, so the pointer can be resolved by search rather than by reading."
